overview: Therizinosaurus cheloniformis is known primarily from enormous claws — the longest manual claws of any known animal, reaching nearly 1 metre along their outer curve. Found in the Late Cretaceous Nemegt Formation of Mongolia (~70 Ma), the animal was initially described as a giant turtle-like creature before additional material from relatives (therizinosaurs from China) revealed its true nature as a large, bizarre herbivorous theropod.

Therizinosaurs represent one of the most dramatic evolutionary reversals in dinosaur history: derived from carnivorous coelurosaur ancestors, they evolved broad hips (convergent with ornithischians), leaf-shaped teeth and long necks suited for browsing vegetation. Therizinosaurus itself may have reached 9–10 metres, making it the largest known therizinosaur.

fossilSites.name: Nemegt Formation
fossilSites.note: Late Cretaceous deposits yielding the massive Therizinosaurus forelimb and claw material.

articles.title: Discovery and initial misidentification
articles.body: Maleev described the enormous claws and forelimb elements in 1954, initially interpreting them as a giant turtle — "cheloniformis" (turtle-form) remains in the species name. Only when well-preserved therizinosaurs were found in China (Alxasaurus, Beipiaosaurus) in the 1980s–90s was it established that Therizinosaurus was a large theropod with a full herbivorous therizinosaur body plan.

articles.title: The giant claws
articles.body: The manual claws of Therizinosaurus are the largest known of any non-avian dinosaur: the outer curve of the first digit claw is estimated at ~80–92 cm in larger specimens. Their function is debated: pulling down branches for feeding (like a giant ground sloth), defence against predators, or display are the main hypotheses. All three are compatible with the herbivorous lifestyle established for therizinosaurs generally.

articles.title: Herbivory in a theropod lineage
articles.body: Therizinosaurs acquired herbivory from a carnivorous ancestor — a profound ecological shift within Theropoda. The transition involved: broadening of the pelvis (to accommodate a larger gut), leaf-shaped teeth for processing vegetation (from the sharp blade-teeth of ancestors), shortening of the skull, lengthening of the neck, and development of a large digestive tract. Beipiaosaurus and Alxasaurus preserve feathers, confirming that therizinosaurs were feathered theropods.

fossilRecord.material: Fragmentary forelimb material, especially enormous manual claws.
fossilRecord.evidence: Giant claws and related therizinosaur skeletons support its unusual herbivorous/omnivorous theropod body plan.

record.description: Therizinosaurus cheloniformis was a giant therizinosaurid from the Nemegt Formation, known mainly from enormous forelimbs and claws plus limited hindlimb material.
facts: No complete skull or skeleton is known.
Herbivory is inferred from close relatives; the five-tonne catalogue mass is too precise for the fragmentary material and is removed.

presentation.heroLead: A giant, long-armed theropod from Late Cretaceous Mongolia, famous for the longest known claws of any land animal and known chiefly from those arms.

animalParagraphs: Therizinosaurus was one of the largest members of Therizinosauria, an unusual group of theropods that turned away from meat-eating. Its forelimbs were enormous: the complete arm of one referred specimen is about 2.4 metres long, and the hand claws reach around half a metre along their curve, the longest known from any land animal.

Almost everything else about its body is inferred. No skull, neck or trunk has been found, so the small head, long neck, wide belly and short tail seen in reconstructions come from better-known relatives such as Erlikosaurus, Segnosaurus and Nothronychus rather than from Therizinosaurus itself. Published lengths of nine to ten metres and masses of several tonnes are extrapolations from the limb bones.

The function of the claws is still debated. Biomechanical modelling by Lautenschlager in 2014 found that the long, slender unguals of Therizinosaurus were poorly suited to digging or forceful strikes and were better matched to hooking and pulling vegetation, although display, defence and intraspecific combat cannot be excluded.
animalHighlights: Hand claws up to roughly 50 centimetres long on arms about 2.4 metres in length are directly measured from fossils.
Its herbivorous, wide-bodied build is inferred from the anatomy of smaller, better-known therizinosaurids.
Modelling suggests the slender claws were suited to hooking and pulling branches rather than to fighting or digging.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: No skull or teeth are known. Herbivory rests on the beaked, small-toothed skulls and wide guts of other therizinosaurids.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: The stout hindlimb bones and four weight-bearing toes are consistent with a slow, upright biped, as in other therizinosaurids.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Only the forelimbs and parts of the hindlimb are measured; whole-body length and mass depend on scaling from relatives.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: The arms are well known; the skull shape, neck length, plumage and colour are not preserved for this genus.

whereFacts.label: Type locality
whereFacts.value: Nemegt Basin, Ömnögovi Province, southern Mongolia

locality.name: Nemegt Basin
locality.note: Nemegt Formation. The holotype was collected by a Soviet–Mongolian expedition in 1948; later Mongolian and joint expeditions recovered the referred forelimb and hindlimb material from the same formation.

presentation.classificationSummary: Therizinosaurus is the name-giving member of Therizinosauridae, a group of coelurosaurian theropods that evolved a plant-eating body plan. Its position within the family is stable, but its fragmentary remains limit how many characters it contributes to phylogenetic analyses.

related.reason: A smaller therizinosaurid with a well-preserved skull that supplies the head anatomy Therizinosaurus lacks.
Another Mongolian therizinosaurid known from jaws, pelvis and limbs that inform the reconstructed body plan.
A contemporary Nemegt giant that was also long known only from enormous arms until more complete material emerged.

questions.title: What did its head look like?
questions.copy: No cranial material is known. The small, beaked head shown in reconstructions is borrowed from Erlikosaurus and other relatives.

questions.title: What were the claws for?
questions.copy: Biomechanical modelling favours hooking and pulling vegetation, but display, defence and other uses remain possible and are not directly testable from the fossils.

questions.title: How big was it really?
questions.copy: Length and mass estimates scale the arms and hindlimb against smaller therizinosaurids; the catalogue carries no mass figure because none can be measured directly.

review.ageReviewNote: All secure material is Maastrichtian Nemegt Formation.

residualUncertainty: Size, skull anatomy and claw function remain uncertain.

evidence.material: Partial forelimbs with giant manual unguals and limited hindlimb remains.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Mass is cleared; most of the body is reconstructed from relatives.
evidence.summary: Therizinosaurus cheloniformis was a giant therizinosaurid from the Nemegt Formation, known mainly from enormous forelimbs and claws plus limited hindlimb material.

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.institution: Palaeontological Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences, Moscow
specimens.note: Several giant manual unguals, a metacarpal fragment and rib fragments collected in 1948; originally interpreted by Maleev as a turtle-like reptile.

specimens.name: Referred forelimb
specimens.institution: Institute of Palaeontology, Mongolian Academy of Sciences, Ulaanbaatar
specimens.note: A largely complete forelimb with scapulocoracoid, humerus, radius, ulna and hand, described by Barsbold in 1976 and the main basis for the reconstructed arm.

specimens.name: Referred hindlimb material
specimens.institution: Institute of Palaeontology, Mongolian Academy of Sciences, Ulaanbaatar
specimens.note: Partial hindlimb described by Perle in 1982 that first linked the arms to a theropod body plan.

panel.headline: Giant arms and claws, a partial hindlimb, and no skull.
panel.standfirst: Therizinosaurus is known from a handful of Nemegt Formation specimens dominated by forelimb bones and enormous hand claws. Limited hindlimb material is referred to it; the skull, neck, trunk and tail have never been found.

coverage.label: Low
coverage.basis: Forelimbs are well represented and a partial hindlimb is referred, but there is no skull, vertebral column, pelvis or associated skeleton, and the specimens come from separate finds.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The holotype consists of giant hand claws with a metacarpal fragment and ribs. A referred specimen preserves a nearly complete forelimb, including the shoulder girdle, and a further specimen preserves part of a hindlimb and foot.
knownRemains.note: Because the material comes from separate finds with no overlapping skeleton, the referral of the hindlimb rests on size and Nemegt provenance rather than on direct association with the claws.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: None known. Head anatomy is reconstructed entirely from other therizinosaurids.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: No vertebrae are securely known; only rib fragments accompany the holotype claws.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Scapulocoracoid, humerus, radius, ulna, metacarpals, phalanges and giant unguals from the forelimb; partial tibia, fibula, ankle and foot bones from the hindlimb.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: None. No skin, feathers, keratin sheaths or gut contents are preserved.

specimenCards.title: PIN 551-483 · holotype
specimenCards.description: Several enormous manual unguals with a metacarpal fragment and ribs, collected by the 1948 Soviet–Mongolian expedition. Maleev described them in 1954 as belonging to a giant turtle-like reptile, which is why the species is called cheloniformis.
specimenCards.meta: Nemegt Formation · Ömnögovi Province · Palaeontological Institute, Moscow

specimenCards.title: IGM 100/15 · referred forelimb
specimenCards.description: A nearly complete forelimb about 2.4 metres long with the shoulder girdle, described by Barsbold in 1976. It established that the claws belonged to a theropod with long arms and three-fingered hands.
specimenCards.meta: Nemegt Formation · Institute of Palaeontology, Ulaanbaatar

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Giant hand claws, a near-complete forelimb with shoulder girdle, rib fragments and part of a hindlimb and foot, all from the Nemegt Formation.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A very large therizinosaurid whose slender claws were probably used to hook and pull vegetation; body form and herbivory are inferred from smaller relatives with skulls and bodies preserved.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Skull, teeth or beak, neck, trunk, pelvis and tail; body length, mass, plumage, colour and whether all referred specimens represent one species.
